Case report 
A case report on pyelovesicostomy of PUJO of pelvic crossed fused renal 
ectopia with single ureter 
Abeselom Lemma Gebreamlak, Kewani Tekelebirhan Alema *, Ibsa Daba Kumsa, 
Messay Mokennen Molla 
Addis Ababa University, School of Medicine, Department of Surgery, Urology Unit, PO BOX: 9086, Ethiopia 
ARTICLE INFO 
Keywords: 
Pyelovesicostomy 
Crossed-fused ectopic kidney 
ABSTRACT 
Introduction: A pyelovesicostomy is a rare procedure that offers an alternative to difficult pyeloplasty or failed 
pyeloplasty in the case of PUJO of pelvic renal ectopia. In this case report, we utilized pyelovesicostomy for a 
dilated renal pelvis of a crossed fused ectopic pelvic kidney with a single ureter. 
Case presentation: This is a 19-year-old male patient who received a diagnosis of pelvic ectopic kidney disease of 
4 years duration. He was on a periodic DJ-stent exchange every 3 months at a different hospital. Upon presentation, the patient complains of pain in the right lower quadrant and a decrease in urine output. On physical 
examination, a palpable mass is detected in the right lower quadrant. The laboratory reveals an elevated 
creatinine level of 2.3 mg/dl. He was admitted with a diagnosis of acute kidney injury and a crossed fused ectopic 
pelvic kidney with Pelvic-Ureteric Junction Obstruction and a migrated Double-J stent. Initially, a semi-rigid 
ureteroscope guided the migrated DJ-stent, which was successfully removed and a new one was inserted. 
Later, an open surgery with a pyelovesicostomy was performed. Subsequently, the patient improved and was 
discharged.

Discussion: Pyelovesicostomy is an ideal treatment option for pelvic ureteral junction obstruction in congenital 
pelvic kidneys. The pyelovesicostomy should not be prone to strictures at the anastomotic site as long as it makes 
wide anastomosis, and the free reflux that results from the surgery shouldn't impair renal function. 
Conclusion: Pyelovesicostomy is feasible, safe, and a potential treatment option for congenital-ectopic pelvic 
kidney with ureteric obstruction. 
1. Introduction 
Pyelovesicostomy was first mentioned in 1929 in relation to an 
ectopic pelvic kidney, but Herwig and Konnak later reported it as a 
different reconstructive method in cases of ureteral obstruction after 
renal transplantation [1]. Pyelovesicostomy cases are rarely reported in 
the literature. The majority of these procedures have been carried out in 
situations of kidney transplant or ectopic pelvic kidney with ureteral 
obstruction [1]. It offers an alternative to difficult pyeloplasty or failed 
pyeloplasty in the case of PUJO of pelvic renal ectopia. 
The population that underwent the pyelovesicostomy should not be 
associated with strictures at the anastomotic site, and any free reflux 
that may arise from the surgery should not impair kidney function. A 
review of the literature revealed no evidence of anastomotic postoperative stricture. The most likely explanation is the widespread 
anastomosis of the bladder and renal pelvis [2]. 
In this case report, we did a pyelovesicostomy for a patient with a 
hugely distended renal pelvis and a crossed fused ectopic pelvic kidney 
with a single ureter. Subsequently, the patient is improved, and on the 6- 
month follow-up, the patient has no pain, normal creatinine (cr-0.5 mg/ 
dl), no episodes of upper urinary tract infection, and a decrease in the 
dilation of the renal pelvis (from severe hydronephrosis to mildmoderate hydronephrosis). These works have been reported in accordance with SCARE criteria [3]. 
2. Presentation of the case

This 19-year-old male patient came from a rural area. He presented 
to the Tikur Anbessa specialized hospital (TASH) urology emergency 
unit with complaints of right lower quadrant pain and a decreased urine 
amount of 1 week's duration. He was told he had an ectopic kidney four 
years ago at St. Paul's specialized hospital after he presented with right

lower quadrant abdominal pain. He was on a periodic DJ-stent exchange 
every 3 months for one year at the same hospital. While he was on DJ 
stent exchange, the DJ stent was migrated to the renal pelvis and was 
referred to the TASH urology emergency unit as having a migrated stent 
because of a lack of an URS instrument. He had no history of smoking, 
recreational drug use, developmental delay, or a family history of such 
illnesses.

At his presentation to our hospital, his vital signs were stable, and 
there was an ill-defined palpable mass in the right lower quadrant. He 
was investigated with a baseline investigation with a complete blood 
count (CBC) in the normal range, serum electrolyte in the normal range, 
urine analysis (UA) normal, and creatinine (Cr) 2.3 mg/dl. On an 
abdominal pelvic ultrasound, it was concluded that he had a fused 
ectopic pelvic kidney with a stent inside the pelvis, disproportional 
dilated renal pelvis, and an abdominal NCCT from referral suggestive of 
an ectopic pelvic kidney with a migrated stent inside the renal pelvis and 
disproportional dilated extra renal pelvis. 
The patient was admitted to the hospital with a diagnosis of acute 
kidney injury (AKI) due to a crossed fused ectopic pelvic kidney with 
Pelvis-Ureteric Junction Obstruction (PUJO) and a migrated Double-J 
(DJ) stent. Initially, a semi-rigid ureteroscope procedure was performed using a 9.5/8 fr scope, during which the migrated stent was 
successfully removed and a new one was inserted using a guidewire. 
However, during this procedure, only the left ureteral opening (UO) was 
visible, and the right UO could not be found. On subsequent days, his 
urine amount was more than 2 litters, and his Cr became 0.5 mg/dl. 
Then, CT-urography was done, suggesting a disproportional dilated 
renal pelvis crossed by a fused ectopic pelvic kidney with a single ureter, 
delayed execration, and a well-positioned DJ-stent in situ (Fig. 1). 
The patient underwent an open pyelovesicostomy after 1 week, with

intraoperative findings of marked distension of the renal pelvis of a 
fused ectopic pelvic kidney. A fairly wide pyelovesico anastomosis was 
done on the dependent area of the pelvis and the distended bladder. Djstent inserted in the pyelovesico anastomosis (Fig. 2). 
Postoperatively, the patient underwent cystourography after 6 
weeks, which revealed decreasing dilatation of the renal pelvis, 
improved drainage of the pelvic kidney with vesicopelvic reflex, and 
residual hydronephrosis (Fig. 3). 6 weeks postoperatively, the DJ stent 
was removed via cystoscopy without any difficulty. The Pyelovesico 
anastomosis site was checked via cystoscope for its patency and wideness. The patient is free of pain, has no episodes of upper urinary tract 
infection (UTI), and has been following up with a renal function test and 
abdominal ultrasound. On follow-up, Cr 0.5 and imaging suggest a residual mild-to-moderate hydronephrosis. 
3. Discussion 
Crossed ectopia with fusion is a very rare case, with an estimated 
occurrence of 1 in 1000 live births. Most individuals with crossed 
ectopic anomalies present no symptoms. These anomalies are often 
discovered incidentally at an autopsy, during routine perinatal ultrasound, or during imaging for another clinical indication. When symptoms occur, they usually develop in the third or fourth decade of life, and 
they include vague lower abdominal pain, pyuria, hematuria, and UTI. It 
is believed that the abnormal kidney position and the anomalous blood 
supply may impede drainage from the collecting system, creating a 
predisposition to UTI and calculus formation. 
In this case report, we did pyelovesicostomy as an optional management of PUJO in crossed fused pelvic renal ectopia instead of dysmembrane pyeloplasty, which is technically unsatisfactory due to 
factors like malrotation of the pelvicalceal system and multiple aberrant 
vessels.

Pyelovesicostomy is an ideal option to consider for the treatment of 
ureteral obstruction in a congenital pelvic kidney or a renal allograft. 
Further indications have included low-grade malignancies of the renal 
pelvis, ureteral injury following pyeloplasty, and to aid in the passage of 
renal stones [1]. 
Because of the excellent short- and long-term results of pyelovesicostomy, this procedure should be considered an excellent alternative to 
pyeloureterostomy, ureteroureterostomy, and ureteroneocystostomy in 
the reconstruction of the upper urinary tract. In pyelovesicostomy, there 
has been no deterioration in renal function attributed to obstruction at 
the anastomotic site or to the free reflux between the bladder and renal 
pelvis. 
The downsides of pyelovesicostomy may include the possibility of 
bacterial cystitis progressing to pyelonephritis and pelvic discomfort 
with a full bladder [1]. Despite the presence of urinary reflux following 
the procedure, no functional, anatomical, or physiological complications appear to exist that would demonstrate not using this procedure 
more frequently in difficult reconstructive cases such as difficulty pyeloplasty or failure dysmembrane pyeloplasty [4]. Pyelovesicostomy is an 
excellent reconstructive surgery option when pyeloplasty is difficult or 
fails. The risk of post-pyelovesicostomy stricture is very rare, as long as 
the pyelovesicostomy anastomosis site is wide [2]. The reflux nephropathy or renal insult is, as such, not critical after pyelovesicostomy 
if you follow the patient with proper treatment of the upper urinary tract 
infection. 
4. Conclusion 
Pyelovesicostomy is feasible, safe, and a potential treatment option 
for congenital-ectopic pelvic kidney with ureteral obstruction in difficult 
reconstructive pyeloplasty or failed pyeloplasty. If we have used a wide 
pyelovesicostomy anastomosis, the risk of stricture at the anastomosis 
site has so far not been reported. Even though urine reflux after the

procedure is inevitable, anatomic or functional renal deterioration is not 
critical. Anatomical or functional complications of the kidney are 
decreased by rapid clinical follow-up of the patient and active infection 
therapy, since episodes of infection brought on by urine reflux increase 
the risk of renal degeneration.
